genZNote: A quieter cousin of Proteus — same urease-positive, ammonia-producing lifestyle, but usually shows up in mixed or catheter-associated infections rather than headlining its own outbreak.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human and animal GI tract, soil, and water
habitat.hostAssociation: Can be part of normal gut microbiota in small numbers; opportunistic nosocomial pathogen
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Found in sewage, soil, and hospital environments

culture.colonyMorphology: Non-lactose-fermenting, translucent colonies on MacConkey agar

identificationClues: Strongly urease-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod, placing it in the same biochemical family (Morganellaceae) as Proteus and Providencia
Positive phenylalanine deaminase test, shared with Proteus and Providencia, helps distinguish this group from other Enterobacterales
Chromosomal inducible AmpC beta-lactamase confers intrinsic resistance to several beta-lactams, similar to Enterobacter and Klebsiella aerogenes
Frequently isolated from hospital-acquired urinary tract infections, wound infections, and bacteremia, often as part of a polymicrobial infection

virulenceFactors: Urease (contributes to struvite stone formation, similar to Proteus)
clinicalImportance.transmission: Nosocomial — catheters, contaminated hospital environment, or endogenous gut flora translocation
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: An underappreciated but not rare cause of hospital-associated infection, particularly in patients with indwelling urinary catheters or recent antibiotic exposure
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Urease positivity plus phenylalanine deaminase positivity groups it biochemically with Proteus/Providencia despite different clinical behavior

examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Urease-positive Enterobacterales relative of Proteus/Providencia, notable for inducible AmpC resistance in hospital settings
